overview: This imported “Mayas” outline covers northern and eastern Yucatán from 1530 to 1650. It does not represent all Maya peoples, a single empire or uninterrupted independence. The period includes Spanish invasion and colonial rule over previously distinct communities. Earlier cities and books explain the region’s inheritance; later testimony shows continuing Maya life. The map boundaries are a rough regional sketch, not a reliable frontier for each year.

periods.title: Before this map: regional Maya powers
periods.summary: Mayapán broke apart in the fifteenth century; smaller states and trading networks continued.

periods.title: Invasions and resistance
periods.summary: Repeated Spanish campaigns established a colony while Maya communities resisted.

periods.title: Colonial Yucatán
periods.summary: New demands for labor and tribute reshaped communities; Maya households and local institutions continued.

items.text: Mayapán was an important northern capital before this map period. Archaeologists studied 205 directly dated skeletons alongside climate evidence. Their research connects fifteenth-century violence with drought and political factionalism, without making weather the sole cause. The city’s political collapse around 1441 to 1461 did not end Maya society: smaller regional states and market networks continued into the sixteenth century.

The earlier city of Mayapán combined impressive defenses with ordinary growing spaces. Its surrounding wall had twelve formal gates, while residential areas included gardens and orchards. Households depended on farming, hunting and exchange as well as city markets. A capital was also a place where people tended useful plants close to home.

At coastal Tulum, most visible buildings date from about 1250 to 1550, reaching into this map period. Walls enclosed three sides, with the Caribbean along the fourth. Five entrances and two watchtowers organized access. Surviving painted rooms and temples show that this trading settlement was also a place of ceremony. Its seaside setting linked it with coastal movement and exchange.

Excavations at Mayapán recovered metal objects and debris from lost-wax casting. Craftspeople made a wax model, formed a mold around it and replaced the wax with molten metal. The raw material came through long-distance exchange. Archaeologist Elizabeth Paris argues that buyers beyond a narrow royal elite could obtain metal goods. These workshops belong to the city’s earlier Postclassic life.

Around 1566, missionary Diego de Landa described palm or straw roofs, rear sleeping rooms and beds of rods topped with mats. He also described children playing with bows and arrows. His account offers household details through a colonial outsider’s often hostile perspective.

Landa describes soaking maize overnight in limewater before grinding it. Travelers and canoe crews carried balls of prepared maize to mix with water in cups made from fruit shells. The ingredients of a portable meal could fit in a bundle: cooking knowledge traveled too.

Animal bones from early colonial Ek Balam reveal changing meals. Introduced pigs and chickens joined local animals, while dog meat remained especially important in the studied assemblage. Researchers connect these food patterns with sixteenth-century labor demands and restrictions on movement. This is evidence from a particular community and deposit, rather than a menu shared by every Maya family.

Later colonial wills, including examples after the map ends, preserve women’s choices about family property. Their bequests included house plots, useful plants, pigs, poultry, bees, clothing and weaving equipment. Some women planned clothes for children or future grandchildren. These documents let historians glimpse family care through ordinary possessions, alongside the inequalities that shaped ownership.

Landa says priests taught their sons and selected sons of leading families to read and write, reckon the calendar, remember history and learn remedies. This describes specialized education. The pupils were training for particular responsibilities; it was not a school system open equally to every child.

For a healing festival in the month Zip, Landa describes practitioners and their wives meeting together. Medicine bundles, figures of Ixchel and divination stones accompanied invocations, dancing and a shared meal. This records a social and religious approach to illness, not proof that a remedy worked.

Maya calendar systems combined different repeating counts. The Haab had eighteen twenty-day months plus five additional days, making 365. The Tzolkin paired twenty day names with thirteen numbers, making a 260-day cycle. Together they formed a Calendar Round repeating after 52 Haab years. Keeping these patterns aligned was a substantial mathematical task.

The Dresden Codex shows what a Maya book could be. The holding library dates it to about 1300 to 1521 in Yucatán. Its thirty-nine leaves form a folded strip of bark-fibre material extending 3.56 meters. Painted signs and images organize ritual, calendrical and astronomical knowledge. To follow its pages, a reader unfolded a long strip rather than turning a bound stack.

A chronicle associated with Nakuk Pech and 1562 is described with the Yucatec Maya words “u belil u kahlail Cħac Xulub Cħen”, translated as “the history and the chronicle of Chacxulubchen”. This is historical Latin-letter spelling, not a rendering of ancient glyphs. Brinton printed the phrase in 1882. Newberry’s catalogue records a photograph of a manuscript copy probably dating to 1840 to 1859, distinguishing the surviving witness from the earlier composition.

Pech’s account also records measuring town land and passing knowledge of boundaries to descendants. It links a family’s place in the landscape with tribute obligations under Spanish rule. Such texts helped local people make claims about land and authority. Pech spoke from a leading family’s position, so his voice should not stand in for everyone in the town.

The Montejo family launched three invasions of northern Yucatán beginning in 1527. Spaniards established Mérida at Tihó in 1542, and a major northeastern Maya revolt was defeated in 1547. Even then, colonial frontiers remained contested. These events changed regional governments; they do not supply one conquest date for every Maya people.

On 12 July 1562, Maní witnessed a public religious prosecution and destruction of Maya sacred objects. Archaeology has added material evidence to the written accounts. During rescue work in 2015, INAH recovered 548 pieces of vessels and incense burners that its researchers associate with that event. These are fragments of damaged objects, not a count of complete vessels.

Maya people continue to speak many languages, raise families, create art and study their own history. Yucatec Maya archaeologist José Huchim Herrera expresses this continuity as “Weyano’one”, translated “we are here”. His work connects present-day expertise with ancestral places. The people represented by these histories belong in the present as well as in museum displays.

ending.text: Spanish conquest transformed northern Yucatán’s governments during the sixteenth century. It did not end Maya communities, languages or historical memory. The imported endpoint of 1650 marks neither a shared political collapse nor the disappearance of a people; Maya life continues today.
